title: The Key to Motivating Students--and Maybe Everyone Else Too
author: Natalie Wexler
summary: Natalie Wexler challenges the common teaching assumption that motivation must come first, before achievement can follow. Citing a four-year study of roughly 1,500 elementary students that tracked both self-reported math motivation and actual achievement, she highlights the counterintuitive finding that achievement consistently predicted later motivation, while motivation did not reliably predict later achievement -- suggesting the causal arrow mostly runs the opposite direction from what many educators assume. She extends the idea beyond the classroom via Matt Yglesias's account of small, measurable weightlifting progress keeping him motivated to keep exercising, framing motivation as a positive feedback loop: achievement produces a feeling of accomplishment, which produces the expectation of future reward, which produces motivation for another round of effort. On the practical question of how to start that loop, Wexler discusses research complicating the simple 'intrinsic good, extrinsic bad' framing of rewards, arguing extrinsic rewards can help unmotivated learners initiate the loop even if intrinsic rewards sustain it later. She closes with a study showing that simply making lessons clearer -- not more motivating -- produced students who did better on tests and reported feeling more motivated, concluding that clear teaching is itself one of the most direct routes to student motivation.
points: Wexler's headline finding -- achievement predicts motivation more reliably than motivation predicts achievement -- inverts a common-sense assumption most teachers hold about the order of cause and effect in the classroom.

The Yglesias weightlifting anecdote generalizes the finding beyond K-12 education, suggesting the achievement-motivation feedback loop applies to adult habit-formation generally, not just to students.

Her nuanced treatment of extrinsic vs. intrinsic rewards -- extrinsic rewards can *initiate* a motivational loop even if they don't sustain it -- pushes back against the simplistic 'extrinsic rewards are always bad' shibboleth common in education discourse.

The clear-vs-unclear lesson study is the piece's strongest practical payoff: it shows lesson clarity itself, not extra motivational effort, produced both better test performance and higher reported motivation in the same experiment.
quotes: Teachers try to motivate students in all sorts of ways: maximizing their choice of reading material, devising math problems that relate to their own lives, giving out gold stars, praising effort.
The finding? Achievement consistently predicted motivation, but motivation did not predict achievement. So the best way to motivate students may be to enable them to experience achievement.
Achievement yields a feeling of accomplishment, which in turn leads to an expectation that future learning will provide a similar reward.
The authors observe that offering students extrinsic rewards can be an effective way of helping unmotivated students initiate a positive feedback loop.
The students who got the clear lesson not only did better on the test but also reported being more motivated.
So if you want to motivate students, it really helps to make your teaching as clear as possible.
